claim: V600E in the BRAF hydrophobic activation segment (AS) pocket accounts for >95% of all kinase mutations.
source: V600E in the BRAF hydrophobic activation segment (AS) pocket accounts for >95% of all kinase mutations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by reference to mutation databases.

claim: BRAF is a serine/threonine protein kinase that is an upstream regulator of cellular responses such as cell division and differentiation and is mediated by the MEK/ERK signaling pathway.
source: BRAF is a serine/threonine protein kinase that is an upstream regulator of cellular responses such as cell division and differentiation and is mediated by the MEK/ERK signaling pathway (Garnett and Marais, 2004; Wellbrock et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garnett and Marais, 2004 and Wellbrock et al., 2004.

claim: BRAF kinase is found mutated in both germline diseases (e.g. cardiofaciocutaneous and Noonan syndromes) and somatic cancers of the thyroid, skin, colon, and lung.
source: BRAF kinase is found mutated in both germline diseases (e.g. cardiofaciocutaneous and Noonan syndromes; (Rauen, 2013) and somatic cancers of the thyroid, skin, colon, and lung (Holderfield et al., 2014; Ascierto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rauen, 2013; Holderfield et al., 2014; and Ascierto et al., 2012.

claim: BRAF is autoinhibited in a closed conformation by the interaction of the N-terminal conserved region 2 with the kinase domain, mediated by the interaction of two phosphorylated residues, Ser365 and Ser729, with a 14-3-3 dimer.
source: BRAF is autoinhibited in a closed conformation by the interaction of the N-terminal conserved region 2 (following the Ras-binding and cysteine-rich domains) with the kinase domain, mediated by the interaction of two phosphorylated residues, Ser365 and Ser729, with a 14-3-3 dimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Brummer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brummer et al., 2006 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon dephosphorylation of the N-terminal phosphorylated Ser365 by phosphatase PPII, the Ras-binding domain is free to interact with Ras at the plasma membrane.
source: Upon dephosphorylation of the N-terminal phosphorylated Ser365 by phosphatase PPII, the Ras-binding domain is free to interact with Ras at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of BRAF activation based on established knowledge.

claim: Phosphorylation in the AS at Thr599 and Ser602 results in kinase activation.
source: subsequent phosphorylation in the AS at Thr599 and Ser602 results in kinase activation (Taylor and Kornev, 2011; Hmitou et al., 2007; Zhang and Guan, 2000; for a recent review on the topic see Lavoie and Therrien, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Taylor and Kornev, 2011; Hmitou et al., 2007; Zhang and Guan, 2000; Lavoie and Therrien, 2015.

claim: The BRAF kinase domain has two subdomains comprising a small N-terminal lobe and a large C-terminal lobe.
source: Similar to other kinases, the BRAF kinase domain has two subdomains comprising a small N-terminal lobe and a large C-terminal lobe (Figure 1A) (Scheeff and Bourne, 2005; Roskoski, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scheeff and Bourne, 2005 and Roskoski, 2010, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The N-terminal lobe contains the nucleotide-binding pocket and the phosphate-binding loop, while the C-terminal lobe binds the protein substrates and contains the catalytic loop.
source: The N-terminal lobe contains the nucleotide-binding pocket and the phosphate-binding loop, while the C-terminal lobe binds the protein substrates and contains the catalytic loop.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established kinase architecture.

claim: In the inactive conformation, Val600 is buried in a hydrophobic pocket made by residues from the N-terminal subdomain (Ala497, Phe498, Leu525, Leu485, Phe468, and Val487) and the AS (Leu597, Ala598, and Trp604).
source: In the inactive conformation, Val600 is buried in a hydrophobic pocket made by residues from the N-terminal subdomain (Ala497, Phe498, Leu525, Leu485, Phe468, and Val487) and the AS (Leu597, Ala598, and Trp604) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Substitution of Val600 by charged amino acids (e.g. Glu) disrupts hydrophobic interactions and results in constitutive kinase activation.
source: Substitution of this residue by charged amino acids (e.g. Glu) disrupts these interactions and results in constitutive kinase activation (Wan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wan et al., 2004.

claim: BRAF V600E does not require RAF dimerization or interaction with Ras to be active.
source: BRAF V600E does not require RAF dimerization or interaction with Ras to be active (Poulikakos et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poulikakos et al., 2011.

claim: BRAF V600E has an increased propensity to form dimers.
source: BRAF V600E does not require RAF dimerization or interaction with Ras to be active (Poulikakos et al., 2011) yet has an increased propensity to form dimers (Freeman et al., 2013; Roring et al., 2012; Thevakumaran et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Freeman et al., 2013; Roring et al., 2012; and Thevakumaran et al., 2015.

claim: V600E is the most frequent BRAF somatic cancer mutation (98% in the COSMIC database).
source: The more important hotspot is found in the AS, with V600E being the most frequent BRAF somatic cancer mutation (98% in the COSMIC database) (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Cantwell-Dorris et al., 2011; Sarkozy et al., 2009; Holderfield et al., 2014; Lavoie and Therrien, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the COSMIC database and multiple citations.

claim: Less frequently found mutations at position Val600 are mutations to Asp, Lys, and Arg, which all require two nucleotide substitutions.
source: Less frequently found mutations at position Val600 are mutations to Asp, Lys, and Arg, which all require two nucleotide substitutions (Davies et al., 2002; Lavoie and Therrien, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davies et al., 2002 and Lavoie and Therrien, 2015.

claim: Pairwise correlations of energies derived from active structures or inactive structures show a good overall correlation.
source: Pairwise correlations of energies derived from active structures or inactive structures, respectively, show a good overall correlation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Poor correlations were found when comparing energies from active and inactive structures.
source: In contrast, poor correlations were found when comparing energies from active and inactive structures, supporting the classification of the template structures.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of FoldX energies.

claim: The AS loop between Leu597 and Gly615 is moderately to highly flexible (high B-factors) and consequently is unsolved in many structures.
source: Structural inspection of 28 BRAF structures with different inhibitors showed that the AS loop between Leu597 and Gly615 is moderately to highly flexible (high B-factors) and consequently is unsolved in many structures (Figure 2; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of 28 BRAF structures shown in Figure 2.

claim: Position Val600 is moderately flexible (70% solved in X-ray structures).
source: Position Val600 is moderately flexible (70% solved in X-ray structures).
evidence: This is based on analysis of X-ray structure data.

claim: BRAF V600E phosphorylated MEK at higher levels than wild-type BRAF.
source: After correcting for differences in BRAF expression levels, we found that BRAF V600E phosphorylated MEK at higher levels than wild-type BRAF
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BRAF V600E phosphorylated MEK at similar levels to the double-nucleotide substitutions of V600D and V600K.
source: After correcting for differences in BRAF expression levels, we found that BRAF V600E phosphorylated MEK at higher levels than wild-type BRAF, and as predicted by FoldX, at similar levels to the double-nucleotide substitutions of V600D and V600K.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BRAF V600M and V600A yielded wild-type levels of MEK phosphorylation, suggesting that these are in fact passenger mutations.
source: In contrast, BRAF V600M and V600A yielded wild-type levels of MEK phosphorylation, suggesting that these are in fact passenger mutations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and involves inference about mutation classification.

claim: The V600G mutation is an intermediate MEK activity mutant.
source: Indeed, the V600G mutation, which is also found in the germline and causes CFC syndrome (Champion et al., 2011) is an intermediate MEK activity mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Champion et al., 2011.

claim: Expression of L597Y and V600H mutants in cells resulted in medium and high kinase activity as predicted.
source: Expression of these mutants (L597Y and V600H) in cells resulted in medium and high kinase activity as predicted (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Replacement of V600 by bulkier hydrophobic residues (e.g. Met, Leu, Trp) resulted in weak (V600W) or no kinase activation.
source: Replacement of V600 by bulkier hydrophobic residues (e.g. Met, Leu, Trp) resulted in weak (V600W) or no kinase activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An excellent correlation exists between FoldX predictions and MEK phosphorylation normalized by total BRAF.
source: Considering the energies and parameters discussed above, we observed an excellent correlation between the FoldX predictions and MEK phosphorylation normalized by total BRAF (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ratios between soluble and insoluble BRAF were similar for wild-type and the V600E and V600W mutants.
source: By analyzing the soluble and insoluble fractions from transiently transfected HEK293 cells, we determined that the ratios between soluble and insoluble BRAF were similar for wild-type and the V600E and V600W mutants (Figure 4C,E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fractionation data shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: The V487E and L252E mutants resulted in significantly more insoluble protein.
source: while the V487E and L252E mutants resulted in significantly more insoluble protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fractionation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BRAF F498S protein could only be detected when loaded in a 10-fold excess of lysate compared to wild-type.
source: It is important to note that due to the very low levels of the BRAF F498S protein, it could only be detected when loaded in a 10-fold excess of lysate compared to wild-type (with no separation into soluble and insoluble fractions; Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ratios of BRAF expressed in the soluble and insoluble fractions show an inverse correlation with the folding energies as predicted by FoldX (R2∼0.67).
source: Comparing the ratios of BRAF expressed in the soluble and insoluble fractions (Figure 4E) shows an inverse correlation with the folding energies as predicted by FoldX (Figure 4B; R2∼0.67, assuming for F498S a ratio of BRAF soluble/insoluble >0 and <0.4, ∼0.2; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Despite the low levels of soluble F498S protein, it phosphorylated MEK at approximately the same level as wild-type BRAF.
source: However, despite the low levels of soluble F498S protein, it phosphorylated MEK at approximately the same level as wild-type BRAF (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The V487E and L525E mutants, after normalizing by the total soluble protein gave higher MEK phosphorylation levels than wild-type.
source: while the V487E and L525E mutants, after normalizing by the total soluble protein gave higher MEK phosphorylation levels than wild-type (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Three conservative RASopathy mutations are found in the hydrophobic pocket region (L485F, L485S, and V487G).
source: Indeed, three conservative RASopathy mutations are found in this region (L485F, L485S, and V487G; Rauen, 2013) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rauen, 2013 and data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: In normal growth medium, V600E or V600K with T599A and S602A mutations showed either no change (V600E) or a slight reduction (V600K) in MEK phosphorylation.
source: In normal growth medium, we observed either no change (V600E) or a slight reduction (V600K) in MEK phosphorylation (Figure 4G–H; Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: By opening the AS and preventing its closure, the kinase becomes active, independent of phosphorylation.
source: This suggests that by opening the AS and preventing its closure, the kinase becomes active, independent of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing V600E/K activity with T599A/S602A mutations.

claim: MEK phosphorylation did not change when Glu611 was mutated to Ala in the context of V600E.
source: However, as MEK phosphorylation did not change (Figure 4G–H; Figure 4—figure supplement 6B–C), it is more likely that this salt bridge contributes little or nothing to stabilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 4G-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 6B-C.

claim: The AS loop energy was the highest contributor to the random forest prediction of cancer frequencies (parameter 3; ∼70%).
source: The AS loop energy was the highest contributor to the random forest prediction of cancer frequencies (parameter 3; ∼70% ), while parameters 2 (folding energy active conformation), 4 (nucleotide substitution frequency), 5 (change in codon usage frequency), and 7 (hydrophobic solvation energy) contributed almost equally, and 1 and 6 (destabilization of inactive conformation and the salt bridge) had very little contribution (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by random forest analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Parameters 2, 4, 5, and 7 contributed almost equally to the random forest prediction.
source: The AS loop energy was the highest contributor to the random forest prediction of cancer frequencies (parameter 3; ∼70% ), while parameters 2 (folding energy active conformation), 4 (nucleotide substitution frequency), 5 (change in codon usage frequency), and 7 (hydrophobic solvation energy) contributed almost equally, and 1 and 6 (destabilization of inactive conformation and the salt bridge) had very little contribution (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by random forest analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Parameters 1 and 6 (destabilization of inactive conformation and the salt bridge) had very little contribution to the random forest prediction.
source: The AS loop energy was the highest contributor to the random forest prediction of cancer frequencies (parameter 3; ∼70% ), while parameters 2 (folding energy active conformation), 4 (nucleotide substitution frequency), 5 (change in codon usage frequency), and 7 (hydrophobic solvation energy) contributed almost equally, and 1 and 6 (destabilization of inactive conformation and the salt bridge) had very little contribution (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by random forest analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: V600E is the only single nucleotide substitution that opens the AS through destabilization of autoinhibitory interactions, without significantly impairing the folding of the inactive or active kinase domain.
source: We show that V600E is the only single nucleotide substitution (Asp, Lys, and Arg, require two bases substitutions) that opens the AS through destabilization of autoinhibitory interactions, without significantly impairing the folding of the inactive or active kinase domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined computational and experimental analyses presented in the study.

claim: Mutations requiring three base substitutions (i.e. V600H) have kinase activities similar to V600E.
source: We show that other mutations requiring three base substitutions (i.e. V600H) have kinase activities similar to V600E.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Position Val600 is in a region where the destabilization of the hydrophobic pocket causes activation of the kinase as structural flexibility still allows for proper folding.
source: We show here, that the effect of a mutation on folding depends on the structural flexibility of the respective hydrophobic pocket where the mutated amino acid is located (Figure 6, left side). Position Val600 is in a region where the destabilization of the hydrophobic pocket causes activation of the kinase as structural flexibility still allows for proper folding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined structural and experimental analyses, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Mutations in structurally rigid areas of the hydrophobic pocket only slightly increase the catalytic activity while increasing destabilization, and thus rapidly cause unfolding of BRAF.
source: In contrast, those mutations in structurally rigid areas of the hydrophobic pocket only slightly increase the catalytic activity while increasing destabilization, and thus rapidly cause unfolding of BRAF (Figure 6, right side).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined structural and experimental analyses, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Whether or not BRAF-activating mutations are found in disease depends on the properties of the AS, the associated possibility of disturbing these properties in a single nucleotide substitution and the impact on the stability of the active and inactive conformations.
source: Altogether, we propose that whether or not BRAF-activating mutations are found in disease depends on the properties of the AS, the associated possibility of disturbing these properties in a single nucleotide substitution and the impact on the stability of the active and inactive conformations.
evidence: This is a conclusion synthesizing the findings of the study.

claim: Rare mutations can be passengers or drivers, depending on the number of base substitutions needed.
source: Rare mutations can be passengers or drivers, depending on the number of base substitutions needed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about nucleotide substitution requirements.

claim: Individuals with silent mutations at critical hotspot positions may acquire rare disease mutations infrequently found in cancer.
source: Additionally, individuals with silent mutations at critical hotspot positions may acquire rare disease mutations infrequently found in cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Mutations that both activate and slightly destabilize a protein may be rescued by random fluctuations in the chaperone levels present in a population.
source: Finally, mutations that both activate and slightly destabilize a protein may be rescued by random fluctuations in the chaperone levels present in a population (Lehner, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lehner, 2013 and involves speculation about rescue mechanisms.

claim: The BRAF kinase domain contains an N-terminal region with a Ras-binding domain, which is followed by a cysteine-rich motif and a C-terminal kinase domain.
source: BRAF contains an N-terminal region with a Ras-binding domain, which is followed by a cysteine-rich motif and a C-terminal kinase domain.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge of BRAF architecture.

claim: The two lobes of the BRAF kinase domain are spatially connected through the AS and can move relative to each other in order to open or close the cleft.
source: The two lobes, which are spatially connected through the AS, can move relative to each other in order to open or close the cleft.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established kinase architecture.

claim: AS residues undergo hydrophobic interactions with the phosphate-binding loop and the 'αC helix' of the N-terminal lobe, locking the kinase in its inactive state.
source: AS residues undergo hydrophobic interactions with the phosphate-binding loop and the 'αC helix' of the N-terminal lobe (making the 'hydrophobic pocket'), locking the kinase in its inactive state.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description based on structural knowledge.

claim: The misalignment of spatially conserved hydrophobic residues in the N- and C terminal lobes ('hydrophobic spines') prevents catalytic activation.
source: In addition, the misalignment of spatially conserved hydrophobic residues in the N- and C terminal lobes ('hydrophobic spines') prevents catalytic activation (Lavoie and Therrien, 2015; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lavoie and Therrien, 2015 and Hu et al., 2015.

claim: Phosphorylation within the AS causes structural rearrangements of the AS, the αC helix and the phosphate-binding loop, reorienting the catalytic Asp of the DFG motif in a catalysis-competent orientation.
source: Phosphorylation within the AS causes structural rearrangements of the AS, the αC helix and the phosphate-binding loop, reorienting the catalytic Asp of the DFG motif in a catalysis-competent orientation, thereby causing BRAF to become active.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description based on established knowledge of kinase activation.

claim: Mutations in the phosphate-binding loop (residues 464 to 472) correspond to <1% of all BRAF mutations in cancer.
source: Mutations in the phosphate-binding loop (residues 464 to 472) correspond to <1% of all BRAF mutations in cancer.
evidence: This is based on mutation frequency data from cancer databases.

claim: The AS belongs to a region within the kinase domain (intra domain region) that has a large tendency to be disordered.
source: This confirms previous predictions that the AS loop belongs to a region within the kinase domain (intra domain region) that has a large tendency to be disordered (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2015 and structural analysis.

claim: Enhanced-sampling structure-based computational simulations proposed that the AS exhibited a significant tendency to switch from the ordered to unstructured conformation.
source: Also, previous enhanced-sampling structure-based computational simulations proposed that the AS exhibited a significant tendency to switch from the ordered to unstructured conformation (Marino et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marino et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations in regions of high flexibility will have less impact on the unfolding of BRAF compared to those in conformational restricted regions.
source: Mutations in regions of high flexibility will have less impact on the unfolding of BRAF compared to those in conformational restricted regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural flexibility analysis.

claim: The overall energy changes (△△G BRAF_inactive) as well as the energy changes in the AS loop alone (△△G BRAF_inactive_loop) have very poor correlations with the occurrence of the corresponding mutation in tumors.
source: The overall energy changes (△△G BRAF_inactive) as well as the energy changes in the AS loop alone (△△G BRAF_inactive_loop) that result from the introduction of mutations in the inactive structure, have very poor correlations with the occurrence of the corresponding mutation in tumors (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Mutations that destabilize the inactive conformation will drive the protein into a complex with chaperones (i.e. HSP90) and/or aggregation/degradation, thereby decreasing its overall effective concentration.
source: First, mutations that destabilize the inactive conformation (△△G BRAF_inactive) will drive the protein into a complex with chaperones (i.e. HSP90; Grbovic et al., 2006) and/or aggregation/degradation, thereby decreasing its overall effective concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grbovic et al., 2006 and involves inference about protein stability effects.

claim: Mutations that destabilize the active conformation will result in the protein having a decreased effective concentration.
source: Second, mutations that destabilize the active conformation (△△G BRAF_active) will also result in the protein having a decreased effective concentration (unless they favor heterodimer formation and cause paradoxical activation (Heidorn et al., 2010; Poulikakos et al., 2010)).
evidence: This claim involves inference about protein stability effects, with citations to Heidorn et al., 2010 and Poulikakos et al., 2010 for the exception.

claim: Unfavorable energy changes in the AS loop of the inactive structures will favor its release and therefore kinase activation.
source: Third, unfavorable energy changes in the AS loop of the inactive structures will favor its release and therefore kinase activation (△△G BRAF_inactive_loop).
evidence: This is an inference based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: Mutating Lys601 to Glu could lead to interaction with Arg575, with a small conformational change.
source: Structural inspection after superimposing all kinases suggests that mutating Lys601 to Glu could also lead to interaction with Arg575, with a small conformational change (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Position 600 always points away from Arg575 in the active conformation, irrespective of if it is a Val or Glu.
source: This did not apply to position 600, however, which always points away from Arg575 in the active conformation, irrespective of if it is a Val or Glu, similar to the equivalent position in many other active kinases (Figure 4—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the V600E structure, Glu600 forms a salt bridge with Lys507 in the αC helix.
source: Finally, although in the V600E structure (PDB entry 4MNF) Glu600 forms a salt bridge with Lys507 in the αC helix (Haling et al., 2014), both residues are solvent exposed, and the Lys side chain is not structurally constrained.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of PDB entry 4MNF, cited from Haling et al., 2014.

claim: The possible salt-bridge energy contribution between Glu600 and Lys507 is negligible.
source: Therefore, the possible salt-bridge energy contribution is negligible (FoldX energy calculations suggest no energetic contribution between Glu600 and Lys507 (△△G (E600A) = 0.04+/- 0.1 kcal/mol).
evidence: This claim is based on FoldX energy calculations.

claim: Mutations to Lys or Arg at position 600 are as activating as Glu and Asp.
source: This explains why mutations to Lys or Arg are as activating as Glu and Asp.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and energetic analysis.

claim: The lower frequency of V600K and V600D mutants in cancer is due to the fact that two base substitutions are needed, whereas only one is needed for V600E.
source: The fact that we found V600K and V600D mutants to be as active as the V600E mutant supports the hypothesis previously published (Davies et al., 2002) that the lower frequency of these mutants in cancer must be is due to the fact that two base substitutions are needed for changing Val600 into Lys or Asp, whereas only one is needed for V600E.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Davies et al., 2002.

claim: If a frequent codon is mutated to a rare one, this could affect translation efficiency and protein levels.
source: If a frequent codon is mutated to a rare one, this could affect translation efficiency and protein levels (Lampson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lampson et al., 2013.

claim: The importance values of the seven different parameters were similar between sets, suggesting that the presence or absence of V600E did not affect the training outcome.
source: The importance values of the seven different parameters were similar between sets, suggesting that the presence or absence of V600E did not affect the training outcome (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on random forest analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
